ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> We recruited 251 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in an online study.

> Participants completed seven randomly ordered items (α = .88) from the Empathic Concern subscale (sample item: "I often have tender, concerned feelings for people less fortunate than me") of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 2011).

> We recruited 502 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.

> Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions manipulating perceived ChatGPT capacity for empathy.

> We recruited 750 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.

> Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions manipulating prior emotional support.

> Participants were aware that J.S. was a hypothetical person in all three conditions.

> For each set of eyes, participants were told the following: "Imagine this is J.S., who told you they have been having a tough time lately."

> In the "ChatGPT Support" and "Human Support" conditions, participants were additionally reminded that J.S. had "been going to [GPT/another person] for emotional support over the past week."

> All participants were then asked to guess what emotion J.S. was feeling (see Figure 3).

> In Study 3, people were asked to imagine someone who needed empathy, but in this study, participants were given the initials of a real student at the Ohio State University who was experiencing emotional distress (although we did include a fictional manipulation about who/what they received empathy from).

> Participants were presented with a cloud of words-some empathic (e.g., understanding), some un-empathic (e.g., indifferent)-that they clicked to represent how they would act or feel toward K.D. We predicted that people would select the fewest empathic words (and the most un-empathic words) in the AI Empathy condition.

> We recruited 800 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.

> Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four conditions: 1.

> Participants were told that K.D. felt like they didn't really have anyone to talk to for emotional support.

> Participants completed the Empathic Concern subscale from the IRI (α = .86).

> Participants were shown a word cloud consisting of 18 words relating to empathy and 25 words relating to indifference (see Figure 4).

> Participants were told to click on the words that expressed how they would act or feel toward K.D. We intentionally presented more indifference than empathy words and randomly varied the sizes of all words.

> We recruited U.S. participants, but different cultural contexts likely shape differences in empathy offloading and social judgment behaviors.

> Participants in all studies were provided informed consent and were debriefed after the studies.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .14", "ps > .08", "ps > .72", 
"ps < .05", "ps < .004"), Text = c("The Human Support condition was between the other two conditions and was not significantly different from either, ps > .14.", 
"RMET performance in the Human Support condition (M = 7.29, SD = 2.37) was not significantly different from the other two conditions, ps > .08 (see Figure 3).",

)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
```

text.text: Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work.
Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly.
When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others.
Four studies provide evidence for "empathy offloading": when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it.
When AI seems more capable of empathy, people-both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)-report more empathy offloading.

When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others' mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses and more social judgment (Study 4).
Empathic AI might provide emotional support at any time, but it may weaken our ethical and emotional commitments to fellow human beings.
The implications of offloading emotional support may include empathic devaluing and atrophy, moral deskilling, and societal fraying.
Providing others with empathy is virtuous.
It is also hard work.
One good thing about artificial intelligence (AI) is that it reduces hard work, but it may also reduce the virtuous behavior of providing others with empathy.
Like many other time-saving inventions (e.g., calculators, computers), large language models (LLMs) are agents of replacement (Gray et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Like many other time-saving inventions (e.g., calculators, computers), large language models (LLMs) are agents of replacement <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gray et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: They can replace cognitive labor-analyzing complex equations and collating data-but they can also replace emotional labor.
They can listen carefully to people's problems and then sympathize with them to foster emotional support (Ovsyannikova et al., 2025).
text.formatted: They can listen carefully to people's problems and then sympathize with them to foster emotional support <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ovsyannikova et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Because LLMs can provide empathic behaviors, people may outsource those behaviors to AI.
Once we know that someone is going to AI, we may "offload empathy," perhaps giving less effort, attention, or concern to others who need emotional support.
Offloading empathy can change how we interact with each other, and may reduce our ethical commitments to fellow humans.
What do we owe each other?
This is perhaps the most foundational question of ethics (Rawls, 2003; Scanlon, 2000).
text.formatted: This is perhaps the most foundational question of ethics <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Rawls, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Scanlon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: How much do we have a duty to care for others versus to pursue our own self-interest (Batson, 2014; Nagel, 2016; Singer, 2016)?
text.formatted: How much do we have a duty to care for others versus to pursue our own self-interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Batson, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Nagel, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Singer, 2016)</ref>?

text.text: Our genes are inherently selfish, and yet humans can perform incredible acts of compassion, like donating organs to strangers and sacrificing lives to protect comrades and countries.

Most of us will never have the chance to act heroically, but we still express the ethical behaviors of care and compassion by providing empathy to each other (Davis, 1983; Tangney et al., 2007; Zagefka et al., 2011).

text.text: Both philosophers and everyday people agree that providing emotional support to others is morally good (Algoe et al., 2008; Gable et al., 2006) and believe that those who consistently provide compassion to others deserve the label of "hero" (Walker & Frimer, 2007).

text.text: One reason human empathy is ethically celebrated (but see Bloom, 2017) is that it is personally costly.
text.formatted: One reason human empathy is ethically celebrated (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bloom, 2017)</ref> is that it is personally costly.

text.text: Providing empathy is effortful.

It can be emotionally exhausting, uncomfortable, financially taxing, and can lead to burnout and compassion fatigue (Cameron et al., 2019; Hodges & Klein, 2001; Lockwood et al., 2017; Robertson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It can be emotionally exhausting, uncomfortable, financially taxing, and can lead to burnout and compassion fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cameron et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hodges & Klein, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Lockwood et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Robertson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: But the work required to provide empathy is a powerful reason why we praise those who emotionally support others (Inzlicht et al., 2018)-humans generally praise effort (Bigman & Tamir, 2016).
text.formatted: But the work required to provide empathy is a powerful reason why we praise those who emotionally support others <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Inzlicht et al., 2018)</ref>-humans generally praise effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bigman & Tamir, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Providing empathy is often experienced as an ethical duty grounded in one's relationship with someone.

People still feel some obligation to provide empathy to others, even after learning that they have already received some support (Aquino et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2022; Jordan et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2017).
text.formatted: People still feel some obligation to provide empathy to others, even after learning that they have already received some support <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aquino et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hong et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Jordan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Zhang et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: But even in the face of ethical duty, we feel entitled to some emotional self-preservation.
Scholars argue that people should protect their "emotional boundaries" by not providing empathy (Bloom, 2017; Brown, 2021; Sheldon et al., 2010).

text.text: Whether this self-concern is selfish or ultimately ethical (you can't help others if you're too exhausted) is open to debate (Maslach & Jackson, 1981; Neff, 2003), but it is clear that psychologically, people trade off costs to the self against benefits to others (Cameron & Payne, 2011).

text.text: The tension between fulfilling ethical duties versus being emotionally self-protective (or lazy) means that every chance to provide empathy is a trade-off: expend effort and be a virtuous person, or conserve effort and be less virtuous.
This choice is complicated by empathic AI, which can provide empathy to other people without them having to do it, helping save people emotional labor and time.
Humans are usually happy to offload labor.

text.text: Study 1 explores the correlation between self-reported willingness to offload empathy and perceptions of AI as capable of empathy.
Study 2 manipulates whether AI is capable of empathy and tests whether that increases self-reported empathy offloading.
Study 3 tests whether learning that someone has already sought support from AI reduces quasi-behavioral empathic engagement.

Study 4 extends this by comparing empathy offloading across AI, friends, and therapist conditions, exploring whether people's reported moral duty to empathize aligns with their actual empathic responses.

Across all studies, sample recruitment, data exclusion practices, measures, manipulations, and procedures are all reported here in the text, in linked preregistrations, or in the online supplemental materials.
Data were analyzed using R. We preregistered Studies 1, 2, and 3, but accidentally overwrote our pre-registration for Study 4, and so Study 4 should be treated as exploratory.
Study materials are available in the online supplemental files.

If people see AI as capable of providing empathy, would they feel less need to provide empathy themselves?
In this study, people rated 1) how much they believe ChatGPT is capable of providing empathic support, and 2) their willingness to offload empathy to ChatGPT.
We predicted a positive correlation between these ratings.
Participants.
We recruited 251 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in an online study.

We excluded one participant for choosing not to have their data be a part of the analysis and one participant for being younger than 18, leaving a remainder of 249 participants (M age = 38.07; SD age = 12.22; 52.61% Men, 46.59% Women, .80% Other; 68.27% White).

Participants first rated their agreement with three randomly ordered items measuring ChatGPT's capacity to provide empathy ("GPT is capable of providing empathy/being compassionate/understanding pain") from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (7).
These items were adapted from Gray et al. (2007) and were averaged to make a composite score of capacity (α = .90).
text.formatted: These items were adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gray et al. (2007)</ref> and were averaged to make a composite score of capacity (α = .90).

text.text: Participants then rated their agreement with four randomly ordered items (α = .93) measuring willingness to offload empathy to ChatGPT ("I'd rather GPT provide emotional support to someone I know than have them rely on me; If someone seeks empathy from me, I'd prefer they turn to GPT instead; GPT can take over my role in offering emotional support to others; I would offload my empathic responsibilities to GPT") from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (7).
Different people may have different baseline tendencies to provide empathy, so we measured individual differences in empathy as a covariate.

Participants completed seven randomly ordered items (α = .88) from the Empathic Concern subscale (sample item: "I often have tender, concerned feelings for people less fortunate than me") of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 2011).

text.text: Items were rated on a scale from Does not describe me well (A) to Describes me very well (E).

Those who already use AI for empathy might have a different perspective, so we measured how often participants use LLMs like ChatGPT for emotional support from Not at all often (1) to Extremely often (5) as a covariate.

The results show that people who view ChatGPT as capable of providing empathy are more willing to offload empathy to it.
Although perceptions of ChatGPT's empathic capacity were modest, many participants still viewed ChatGPT as a viable source of empathy, and these beliefs predicted offloading.
We also found that using ChatGPT more for empathic support predicted offloading, and that trait empathy was negatively correlated with offloading.
Of course, this study was only correlational, a limitation we now address.

Study 2 experimentally manipulated perceived empathic capacity of ChatGPT using a naturalistic manipulation-real newspaper articles describing the rise of AI being used for empathy-compared to control articles about AI generating images.

We predicted that participants exposed to articles about empathic AI would view ChatGPT as more capable of providing empathy and, in turn, report greater willingness to offload empathic responsibilities to AI.
We also tested whether perceived capacity of ChatGPT for empathy mediated the link between condition and willingness to offload.
Participants.
An a priori power analysis suggested we needed a minimum sample size of 175 per condition to achieve 80% power to detect a small effect size, specified as Cohen's d = .30.
We aimed to get 250 participants per condition to account for possible exclusions.
We recruited 502 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.

We excluded six participants for choosing not to have their data be a part of the analysis, one participant for not consenting, and one participant for being an outlier, leaving a remainder of 494 participants (M age = 37.4; SD age = 12.5; 45.95% Men, 51.82% Women, 2.22% Other; 64.98% White).
Manipulation.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions manipulating perceived ChatGPT capacity for empathy.
In the "AI Image Generation" condition (n = 246), participants viewed news headlines and snippets about AI generating images.
In the "AI Empathy" condition (n = 248), participants viewed headlines and snippets about AI being used for empathy.

All articles were published between January 2024 and April 2025 and were drawn from high-traffic U.S. news outlets (The New York Times, CBS News, The Wall Street Journal, MSN, and Forbes; Similarweb, 2025), presented in random order.

text.text: The results show that reading news articles about empathic AI increased empathy offloading, and this effect was explained by changes in perceived capacity.
The next study extends empathy offloading to two key measurement domains: explicit ratings of moral obligation and more quasi-behavioral measures.
Study 3 was an experiment that compared empathy offloading after someone learned that a sad acquaintance had already received empathy from ChatGPT, a friend, or no one (the control condition).
We predicted more empathy offloading for ChatGPT versus the control condition, but were unsure about the relative offloading between someone receiving support from ChatGPT or another person.
On one hand, people are generally seen as more capable of providing empathy, and our first two studies show that perceived capacity can drive offloading.
On the other hand, when other people provide empathy, it sets some social norms for empathy that others might follow (Algoe et al., 2008).
text.formatted: On the other hand, when other people provide empathy, it sets some social norms for empathy that others might follow <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Algoe et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: We also explored whether empathy offloading might extend beyond self-reports to explicit ratings of moral obligation and to more quasi-behavioral measures.

Given that empathic behavior often involves asking questions (Nils & Rimé, 2012) and engaging with others' expressions and mental states (Bensalah et al., 2016; Decety & Jackson, 2004; Malle & Hodges, 2007; Preston & de Waal, 2002), we included two quasi-behavioral measures: a question-writing task and the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).

text.text: Finally, we measured ratings of emotional pain to test for an alternative hypothesis about empathy offloading: that people infer other people have less pain when they go to AI for empathy.
Participants.
An a priori power analysis suggested we needed a minimum sample size of 223 per condition to achieve 80% power to detect a small effect, specified as η² = .014 or Cohen's f = .12.
We aimed to get 250 participants per condition to account for possible exclusions.
We recruited 750 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.

We excluded seven participants for failing attention checks and/or choosing not to have their data be a part of the analysis, for a remainder of 743 participants (M age = 38.06, SD age = 11.57; 47.24% Men, 50.74% Women, 2.02% Other; 70.70% White).
Manipulation.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions manipulating prior emotional support.
In the "No Support" condition (control; n = 248), participants read the following vignette: "Imagine someone you know, J.S., told you that they have been having a really tough time lately.
It seemed like they want to talk to you."
In the "ChatGPT Support" condition (n = 249), participants read the same vignette but were also told that J.S. "has been going to ChatGPT for emotional support over the past week."

In the "Human Support" condition (n = 246), participants read the same vignette as the "No Support" condition but were also told that J.S. "has been going to another person for emotional support over the past week."
Participants were aware that J.S. was a hypothetical person in all three conditions.
We used the same face-valid measures of perceived ChatGPT empathic capacity (α = .90), empathy offloading, and trait empathy (α = .87) as in Studies 1 and 2.
We also included a more explicit measure of personal responsibility, and two quasi-behavioral proxies for empathy.
The first was asking questions to J.S., and the second was the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test to measure engagement with mental states.
We also included perceptions of J.S.'s emotional pain.

Participants rated their agreement with three randomly ordered items (α = .83) measuring perceived personal responsibility to help J.S. out ("I feel obligated to provide emotional support to J.S.; I feel personally responsible to help J.S.; I feel compelled to talk to J.S.") from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (7).
Participants asked up to five questions to J.S. about their sad situation.
We were especially interested in questions about J.S.'s "emotional situation," reflecting participants' interest in providing empathy.
Three undergraduate research assistants independently coded these questions into two subcategories: questions about J.S.'s emotional situation in general (e.g., "What is bothering you?"
; α = .94) and, given J.S.'s situation, questions about how participants themselves could help out J.S. (e.g., "Do you want me to just sit and listen?"
Fewer questions indicated less emotional effort and more offloading.
Eyes Test (RMET), which asks people to guess the emotions of different people who are represented by only their eyes.

Originally a task developed for autism research, the RMET reflects variation in people's capacity for emotional mental state reading, a skill related to empathy (Decety & Jackson, 2004; Yalçın & DiPaola, 2020).

text.text: While the RMET is traditionally seen as a measure of emotion recognition ability (and we originally preregistered the RMET as a perspective-taking measure), performance on the task also requires attention to and engagement with others' mental states.
We therefore included the RMET to assess whether situational factors, such as prior AI support, might influence how attentive people are to others' mental states.

Prior work has shown that experimentally induced states can shift RMET performance (Harkness et al., 2005 (Harkness et al., , 2010;; Nolte et al., 2013), suggesting the task is sensitive to contextual influences and not solely a fixed trait measure.

text.text: We reasoned that the RMET could also predict differences in engagement across conditions, especially because we selected the 12 most difficult stimuli from the original set of 36 eyes (defined as those with the lowest mean accuracy in emotion identification across both the general population and student samples from the original paper).
The correct emotions for the 12 selected items were: uneasy, cautious, anticipating, doubtful, decisive, tentative, interested, cautious, interested, confident, serious, and concerned.
For each set of eyes, participants were told the following: "Imagine this is J.S., who told you they have been having a tough time lately."
In the "ChatGPT Support" and "Human Support" conditions, participants were additionally reminded that J.S. had "been going to [GPT/another person] for emotional support over the past week."
All participants were then asked to guess what emotion J.S. was feeling (see Figure 3).

text.text: Consistent with predictions, participants showed more empathy offloading after learning that an acquaintance went to AI for support versus not receiving any previous empathic support.
These results were found with self-reports of empathy offloading, with question asking, and with the RMET.
Notably, the RMET emotions span a range of affective states from positive to neutral-cognitive to negative.
Because affective states were not uniformly negative, we reduced the likelihood that the "tough time" framing inflated accuracy through base-rate guessing of negative emotions.
All three conditions received the same "tough time" framing, so any inflation in accuracy would apply equally across conditions and cannot account for the significant differences we observed.
Evidence for differences between AI and human support was limited.
While some measures showed small differences favoring greater offloading in the AI condition, others showed no reliable differences.

Interestingly, participants' explicit ratings of personal responsibility (or perceived emotional pain) were not significantly different across conditions, suggesting that people feel the same ethical responsibility to help someone regardless of any previous support they received.

This mismatch between self-reports and quasi-behavioral outcomes suggests that offloading may happen more implicitly: even if people feel ethically compelled to help someone after they go to empathic AI, their actions showcase less empathy.
The previous studies found evidence for empathy offloading, but still, open questions remain.
First, would we find the same effects for someone less hypothetical?

In Study 3, people were asked to imagine someone who needed empathy, but in this study, participants were given the initials of a real student at the Ohio State University who was experiencing emotional distress (although we did include a fictional manipulation about who/what they received empathy from).
Second, how does empathy offloading for AI compare to other sources of empathy?
To test this, this study included four conditions: an AI empathy condition, a control/no support condition, and conditions where the student received empathy from either friends or a therapist.
We again assessed self-reports of empathy offloading and responsibility.
This study also included a new quasi-behavioral measure of empathy offloading: language selection.

Participants were presented with a cloud of words-some empathic (e.g., understanding), some un-empathic (e.g., indifferent)-that they clicked to represent how they would act or feel toward K.D. We predicted that people would select the fewest empathic words (and the most un-empathic words) in the AI Empathy condition.
We also broadened our focus on empathic AI, discussing AI chat platforms in general instead of ChatGPT specifically, to provide more generalizability.
Participants.
An a priori power analysis suggested we needed a minimum sample size of 134 per condition to achieve 80% power to detect a small effect, specified as Cohen's f = .14.
We aimed to get at least 150 analyzable participants per condition after exclusions.
We recruited 800 participants from CloudResearch Connect to participate in a between-groups study.
Due to general increases in bot farming, we imposed stricter exclusion criteria.

We excluded 59 participants for failing attention checks (i.e., choosing inaccurate scale items to the statement "Choose Somewhat disagree for this statement," choosing an irrelevant answer to the question "In the beginning of the survey, you were asked to read a prompt about K.D. What did we mention about K.D.?"
and/or failing the Müller-Lyer illusion bot-detection checks).

We excluded seven other participants for choosing not to have their data be a part of the analyses and/or failing data quality checks (i.e., completion times that were less than one-third of the median or values exceeding 3.29 standard deviations from the mean).
We had a remainder of 737 participants (M age = 40.28, SD age = 13.97; 42.88% Men, 54.14% Women, 2.98% Other; 68.25% White).

Participants first read the following vignette: "A survey led by the Chief Wellness Officer at the Ohio State University found that many students report feeling emotionally overwhelmed and burned out.
Students are having a tough time managing the stress from juggling course work, jobs, extracurriculars, and their personal lives.
In this survey, we will present one student to you, K.D., who is feeling overwhelmed.
We would like you to answer some questions about them."
Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four conditions: 1.
"No Support" (n = 186).
Participants were told that K.D. felt like they didn't really have anyone to talk to for emotional support.
After the language selection task, participants rated agreements to items about AI chat platforms for the rest of the study, which served as baseline AI perceptions.
"AI Empathy" (n = 178).
Participants read the following: "People often reach out to an AI chat platform for emotional support.
Studies show that AI chat platforms are very effective at providing emotional support.
In fact, a recent research paper from Harvard found that the top use of generative AI in 2025 was for providing therapy and companionship.
Consistent with this, K.D. has reported going to an AI chat platform for empathy.
K.D. has also reported feeling understood and emotionally validated after talking with the AI chat platform."

Only for this condition did we include an additional reference to a recent research paper from Harvard (Zao-Sanders, 2025) to explicitly increase perceptions of AI being commonly used for-and capable of-empathy.
Although this creates an imbalance across conditions, we wanted to overcome current intuitions about AI's inability to offer empathy.
For example, in Study 1, the average rating of ChatGPT's ability to provide empathy was 3.24 out of 7.
"Friends Empathy" (n = 185).
Participants read the following: "People often reach out to close friends for emotional support.
Studies show that friends are very effective at providing emotional support.
Consistent with this, K.D. has reported going to their two closest friends for empathy.
K.D. has also reported feeling understood and emotionally validated after talking with their friends."
"Therapist Empathy" (n = 188).
Participants read the same vignette as when K.D. went to friends, but instead it said "a therapist."
Perceived Capacity for Empathy.

Participants rated the same perceived capacity for empathy items used in Studies 1-3 (α = .95), slightly adapted to refer to the relevant empathy source for each condition ("Friends/Therapists/AI chat platforms are capable of providing empathy/ giving compassionate advice/ understanding pain").
This time, participants rated items from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (6), excluding the "Neither agree nor disagree" option.

Participants rated the same willingness to offload items from Study 1 (α = .92), slightly adapted to refer to the relevant empathy source for each condition ("I'd rather have friends/therapists/AI chat platforms provide emotional support to someone than have them rely on me for support; I'd prefer someone turn to friends/therapists/AI chat platforms for empathy instead of me; Friends/Therapists/AI chat platforms can take over my role in offering emotional support to others; I would offload my responsibilities to give empathy to friends/therapists/AI chat platforms") from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (6).
Participants completed the Empathic Concern subscale from the IRI (α = .86).

Participants rated their agreement with four randomly ordered items (α = .88) measuring their perceived moral duty to provide K.D. empathy ("I feel ethically compelled to provide empathy to them; I think it's a moral imperative to provide emotional support to them; It would be wrong not to listen to their problems; I have a moral duty to help them") from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (6).
Language Selection Task.
Participants were shown a word cloud consisting of 18 words relating to empathy and 25 words relating to indifference (see Figure 4).

text.text: Participants were told to click on the words that expressed how they would act or feel toward K.D. We intentionally presented more indifference than empathy words and randomly varied the sizes of all words.
These design choices required participants to engage in greater visual search to find and select empathy-related words, while indifference words were more visually accessible and easier to click on.
This was done to reflect the finding that expressing empathy can be effortful (Cameron et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This was done to reflect the finding that expressing empathy can be effortful <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cameron et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, we created the word cloud on an online free word cloud generator and gave each word an assigned point value inversely proportional to the size, such that smaller words (harder to find/click on) were worth more points.
We had five sizes, with the biggest sized words being worth 1 point and the smallest sized words 5 points (see Figure 4).

Two indices were computed by combining the weights and clicks of each word category (i.e., Σ(weight*clicks)-one for empathy word selections and one for indifference word selections).

text.text: Discussion and what they actually do.
text.formatted: <head>Discussion</head> and what they actually do.

text.text: People said they were less willing to offload in the AI Empathy condition compared to the Friends and Therapist Empathy conditions.
In the language selection task, however, participants in the AI Empathy condition selected fewer empathy words and more indifference words than all other conditions.
Consistent with all our previous studies, AI's perceived capacity for empathy also strongly predicted willingness to offload to it.
Even though average perceptions of AI's capacity were modest, variation in perceived capacity reliably tracked offloading.

Interestingly, participants selected the most empathy words (and the fewest indifference words) when the student went to friends for support, consistent with the power of social norms to personally provide empathy even if others already have (Algoe et al., 2008; House, 2018).
text.formatted: Interestingly, participants selected the most empathy words (and the fewest indifference words) when the student went to friends for support, consistent with the power of social norms to personally provide empathy even if others already have <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Algoe et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">House, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, moral duty to provide empathy was highest when the student received support from friends, compared to AI, therapists, and no support, which did not differ from each other.
This pattern further highlights that friends set a social norm that heightens perceived relational obligation to provide support.
Another important pattern is the difference between the AI and Therapist conditions, where people may be reducing their empathy giving for different reasons.
Participants reported greater willingness to offload to therapists and perceived them as more capable, yet showed the most indifference when K.D. went to AI.
Offloading to therapists may reflect a rational reduction in empathy to a trusted, socially accepted source.
But the increased selection of indifference words after K.D. went to AI may not only reflect offloading to save empathic effort.

People may also be signaling social judgment, disapproval, or psychological distancing toward the person who sought support from AI (Fehr & Gächter, 2002; Williams, 2007), consistent with participants also rating K.D. as more weird, antisocial, and desperate than in the Friends and Therapist Empathy conditions (see the online supplemental materials).
text.formatted: People may also be signaling social judgment, disapproval, or psychological distancing toward the person who sought support from AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fehr & Gächter, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Williams, 2007)</ref>, consistent with participants also rating K.D. as more weird, antisocial, and desperate than in the Friends and Therapist Empathy conditions (see the online supplemental materials).

text.text: Offloading and social distancing may therefore be operating simultaneously, meaning that the person who turns to AI for support may end up doubly worse off, receiving even less empathy for how they chose to get support.
Philosophers mostly agree that it is ethically good to provide empathy.
It also seems clear that it is a (moral) good for people to receive empathy if they need it.
In other words, when it comes to the question of what we owe each other (Rawls, 2003; Scanlon, 2000; Singer, 2016), we do seem to owe each other some kind of emotional support.
text.formatted: In other words, when it comes to the question of what we owe each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Rawls, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Scanlon, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Singer, 2016)</ref>, we do seem to owe each other some kind of emotional support.

text.text: However, this sense of empathic obligation seems to reduce when we learn that someone has gone to AI for empathic support.
To be sure, there is good in empathic AI, because it allows people to feel supported at all hours of the day with little cost, but our research reveals support for the idea of empathy offloading.
Four studies show that, when AI is seen as capable of providing empathy, it reduces people's willingness to emotionally support people who could go-or who have gone-to AI for empathy.
Study 1 found that people who see AI as more capable of providing empathy are also more willing to offload interpersonal empathy to it.
Study 2 manipulated the perceived capacity of AI and found the predicted effect: when AI was described as more capable of empathy, people offloaded interpersonal empathic support to it.

Studies 3 and 4 provided evidence beyond simple self-report that learning someone sought AI support reduces empathy given to them, including asking fewer questions and engaging less with others' mental states (Study 3), and selecting fewer empathy words and more indifference words in a language selection task (Study 4).
Interestingly, empathy offloading occurred while people explicitly reported having the moral responsibility to provide interpersonal empathy, highlighting a disconnect between what people say and do.
This suggests that empathy offloading may occur more implicitly and intuitively than deliberatively, consistent with models of moral judgment as an intuitive process (Greene, 2014).
text.formatted: This suggests that empathy offloading may occur more implicitly and intuitively than deliberatively, consistent with models of moral judgment as an intuitive process <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Greene, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Scholars disagree about whether AI can authentically provide empathy (Kleinert et al., 2026; Perry, 2023; Rubin et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2024), and science has largely focused on how recipients react to AI empathy: do people trust and benefit from it, does the "AI" label matter to people, and how does AI empathy compare to receiving real human empathy (Inzlicht et al., 2024; Laban & Cross, 2024; Ovsyannikova et al., 2025; Pelau et al., 2021; Wenger et al., 2026; Yam et al., 2023).

text.text: Far less attention has been paid to the downstream consequences of empathic AI-how the rise of AI impacts human connection.

Some work examines how people can feel less empathy when writing AI-assisted empathic messages (Lee et al., 2025), and other work shows that AI can corrupt ethical behavior, such as by increasing dishonesty (Köbis et al., 2021 (Köbis et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Some work examines how people can feel less empathy when writing AI-assisted empathic messages <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Lee et al., 2025)</ref>, and other work shows that AI can corrupt ethical behavior, such as by increasing dishonesty <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Köbis et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Köbis et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Our work suggests that AI can shift ethical behavior between people.
Even if empathic AI is good for recipients in the moment, it may quietly weaken our empathic behaviors without us recognizing it.
Our findings suggest at least two ways empathic AI can reduce human empathy, each with distinct ethical implications: offloading and social judgment.
Studies 1-3 reveal that when people believe that AI can provide empathy, they may put less effort into providing empathy themselves.
Over time, this behavior may lead people to devalue empathy as a morally important emotion.
People intuitively associate value with effort and intention (Inzlicht et al., 2018), and we often devalue the tasks done by AI (Böhm et al., 2023; Lubars & Tan, 2019; Zhang & Gosline, 2023).
text.formatted: People intuitively associate value with effort and intention <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Inzlicht et al., 2018)</ref>, and we often devalue the tasks done by AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Böhm et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Lubars & Tan, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Zhang & Gosline, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: So, when AI provides empathy automatically and effortlessly, people may see offering empathy as cheap, trivial, and ultimately, a less ethically meaningful resource.
The devaluation of empathy may eventually lead to moral deskilling-the gradual loss of human ability to exercise moral judgment and cultivate moral skills, especially empathy.
This stems from increased reliance on technology to perform labor on humans' behalf, paralleling how automation devalues skilled labor in the workforce (Vallor, 2015).
text.formatted: This stems from increased reliance on technology to perform labor on humans' behalf, paralleling how automation devalues skilled labor in the workforce <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Vallor, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: If people increasingly offload their empathy-giving behaviors to AI, they may no longer appreciate all the hard work and kindness that goes into giving and receiving empathy.
Alternatively, when people see others going to AI for empathy, they may also express disapproval for this choice and withdraw empathy as a form of social punishment.

Study 4 revealed that participants in the AI Empathy condition actively selected more indifference words and rated K.D. as more weird, antisocial, and desperate (see the online supplemental materials).

Rather than saving the laborious effort of giving empathy, people may be penalizing the struggling person because they view AI as an unsuitable source of support, and-consequentlywithdrawing their support.

If AI-seeking remains stigmatized, recipients may hide their emotional struggles out of fear of social disapproval, leading to more general loneliness, less help-seeking, and perhaps other social ills.
Societal Fraying.
Society is not a single "thing" but instead a web of connections between people.
These connections are built by social interactions and mutual exchanges of kindness and support (Morelli et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These connections are built by social interactions and mutual exchanges of kindness and support <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Morelli et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet offloading empathy may hinder one of the main ways we maintain social connections: noticing distress and emotionally responding to show that we matter to each other.
If social connection is severed by empathic AI, we may stop feeling like we owe each other love, care, and support.
We may deprive ourselves of emotional intimacy, shared understanding, and feelings of vulnerability that make us human (George et al., 2023; Krapp et al., 2024; Laban & Cross, 2024).
text.formatted: We may deprive ourselves of emotional intimacy, shared understanding, and feelings of vulnerability that make us human <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(George et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Krapp et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Laban & Cross, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We may also grow distant and isolated from each other, feeding into the loneliness epidemic (Office of the Surgeon General, 2023; Twenge et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We may also grow distant and isolated from each other, feeding into the loneliness epidemic (Office of the Surgeon General, 2023; <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Twenge et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As empathy offloading becomes normalized, social norms around relational responsibility may weaken, lowering the ethical commitments we make to each other.
Aristotle argued that moral virtue is developed through repeated practice (Aristotle, 1999, Book II).
text.formatted: Aristotle argued that moral virtue is developed through repeated practice <ref type="bibr">(Aristotle, 1999, Book II)</ref>.

text.text: Empathy may not be a muscle in the traditional sense, but it certainly strengthens with repeated practice and atrophies with decreased use (Shastry et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Empathy may not be a muscle in the traditional sense, but it certainly strengthens with repeated practice and atrophies with decreased use <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Shastry et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If AI replaces empathy, people in all kinds of relationships may lose the ability to practice genuine human empathy.
Likewise, the rise of empathic AI may change how children learn to live.
Some are already worrying that by offloading emotional labor to AI, like writing break-up notes, kids may skip out on the difficult but essential parts of social development (Shirky, 2026).
text.formatted: Some are already worrying that by offloading emotional labor to AI, like writing break-up notes, kids may skip out on the difficult but essential parts of social development <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Shirky, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When the default response to any distress is "go cry to AI," generations may not learn how to connect with others.
Friendships and romantic relationships may also wane if people struggle to open up emotionally and instead run to AI (Ho et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Friendships and romantic relationships may also wane if people struggle to open up emotionally and instead run to AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ho et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Without practicing empathy, we may end up losing our virtues of compassion and care.
It is important to note that our conclusions come with a number of caveats.
Overall Low Perceived Empathic Capacity of AI.

Empathic AI is in its infancy, and accordingly, people gave relatively low ratings for AI's capacity to provide empathy (see Figure S11 in the online supplemental materials for histograms of AI's capacity for empathy across conditions).
text.formatted: Empathic AI is in its infancy, and accordingly, people gave relatively low ratings for AI's capacity to provide empathy (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S11</ref> in the online supplemental materials for histograms of AI's capacity for empathy across conditions).

text.text: These low AI empathy ratings likely explained the relatively low explicit endorsement of empathy offloading after learning that someone went to AI for emotional support, versus a friend or therapist.
Of course, all four studies revealed support for the crucial thesis-that the more people saw AI as capable of empathy, the more they offloaded empathybut we acknowledge these low ratings.
Importantly, this paper attempts to get ahead of the curve of social change by examining the social and ethical phenomenon of offloading empathy to AI before its widespread use.

Consistent with lower perceptions of AI's capacity for empathy, the average amount of empathy offloading was relatively low across Studies 1-3 (M = 2.10-3.27 on a 7-point scale), which could raise concerns about floor effects and violations of normality assumptions underlying parametric tests.
To assess this, we examined skewness and kurtosis values.
Following Curran et al. (1996), skewness values below 2 and kurtosis values below 7 are considered acceptable for parametric testing.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Curran et al. (1996)</ref>, skewness values below 2 and kurtosis values below 7 are considered acceptable for parametric testing.

text.text: Our values fell within these ranges across all studies and all primary measures.
To further confirm robustness for the word cloud task in Study 4, we ran Kruskal-Wallis tests on the equal-weights indices, and all primary findings held.

The low means therefore reflect genuine variation around a low baseline, consistent with the fact that AI empathy is still an emerging phenomenon and people's baseline willingness to offload remains modest.
As discussed in Study 4, the number of indifference word selections in the AI Empathy condition may reflect negative social judgment toward AI-seekers.
However, exploratory analyses of our data suggest the existence of more authentic empathy offloading.

Regression analyses find that offloading was predicted by both perceiving AI as setting a higher empathic standard and by people wanting to put in less effort (see Table S6), consistent with cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) and growing evidence that AI can match or exceed human empathic responses (Ovsyannikova et al., 2025; Wenger et al., 2026).

text.text: Thus, offloading and disapproval may not be mutually exclusive and may even operate simultaneously, but they call for meaningfully different interventions: one focused on restoring felt responsibility, the other on reducing stigma toward AI-seekers.

We also acknowledge a broader limitation of the Language Selection Task: visual search does not directly operationalize interpersonal emotional labor, and the task reflects symbolic effort with minimal real-world consequences.
We also note that empathic expression was the predominant selection of words across all conditions, consistent with the idea of a general ethical obligation to endorse empathy.
As our methods stated, we examined the relative difference between indices across conditions rather than absolute levels.
The between-condition differences should be interpreted as shifts in how much empathy people expressed rather than a wholesale abandonment of empathic engagement.
Future work should use measures that more directly capture empathic labor to establish stronger construct validity and to cleanly isolate mechanisms.

The RMET, a task where participants identify emotions of people shown only by their eyes, is typically treated as a measure of stable individual differences in emotion recognition ability rather than momentary engagement.

While we still observed significant differences in engagement with others' mental states and were able to shift empathic engagement toward an acquaintance who has gone to AI for empathy, the RMET is still an imperfect proxy for the active, interpersonal engagement involved in real-world empathy.
Future work should build on these findings using more targeted measures of empathic engagement and perspective-taking.

In Study 4, where we described a student receiving empathy from AI, we note that this was the only condition where we included an institutional endorsement-a reference to Harvard research identifying therapy and companionship as the top use of generative AI.
This institutional endorsement may have independently and asymmetrically influenced AI's perceived capacity for empathy.

We intentionally designed the vignette in this way to ensure our manipulation was strong enough to test whether capacity leads to offloading, because people's baseline perceptions of AI's empathic capacity were low (Study 1 mean = 3.24/7; Yin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We intentionally designed the vignette in this way to ensure our manipulation was strong enough to test whether capacity leads to offloading, because people's baseline perceptions of AI's empathic capacity were low (Study 1 mean = 3.24/7; <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Yin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We prioritized experimental validity (creating conditions under which offloading could plausibly occur) over perfect symmetry across conditions.

Of course, this tradeoff is a limitation that means that we cannot fully rule out whether the institutional framing contributed to the effects we observed, potentially creating some demand characteristics.

Future work should continue to test offloading effects among participants who already believe that AI can provide empathy with more symmetrically framed vignettes to isolate the effect of support source from the effect of institutional framing.

Participants rated perceived capacity for empathy and empathy offloading from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (7) in Studies 1-3, and from Strongly Disagree (1) to Strongly Agree (6) in Study 4, which may impact interpretability of mean values.

We removed the "Neither agree nor disagree" (4) scale point in Study 4 to encourage participants to choose one side of agreement, since Study 2 had a mean of 4.30 for AI's perceived capacity when participants read newspaper headlines about AI and empathy.
Behavioral science has long debated which effect sizes are meaningful.

Many well-replicated findings in social psychology have small to medium effect sizes (Richard et al., 2003), and some of our effects fall within this range (e.g., d = .45-.63 for Study 2, η² = .005-.009 in Study 3 for perceived capacity and empathy offloading), with not all comparisons reaching significance in Studies 3 and 4.

text.text: While a small effect might suggest that any single encounter with someone who sought AI empathy likely only has a modest impact on the empathy they receive, small effects are not necessarily unimportant.

If people start to learn about struggling others using AI for empathy more often, over time many small independent empathy reductions can sum to a meaningful amount of empathy withheld (Funder & Ozer, 2019).

text.text: Our studies estimate the per-encounter effect, but they do not test how often this situation actually occurs in everyday life, though recent work suggests it is becoming more common (Huang et al., 2026; Zao-Sanders, 2025).

text.text: Future work should test whether such effects accumulate over repeated exposures, both within-person and across populations.
The current research poses many questions, understandably given this paper is among the first to examine the interpersonal consequences of empathic AI.
One obvious future direction is to use more behavioral measures, which is always important for establishing the real-world importance-and robustness-of psychological findings.
Our studies used both self-report ratings and quasi-behavioral measures, but we acknowledge that we did not explore real-time embodied social interactions.
This is only an initial exploration of empathy offloading, and so we encourage other work that explores these effects in more real-world contexts.
Real-world empathy also unfolds between specific people with specific relationships, and likely hinges on who is giving support, who is seeking support, and what they are seeking it for.
Not all observers will respond to someone seeking AI emotional support in the same way.

Observers who are averse to AI or who have less in common with AI-seekers are likely to judge them more harshly, while those who personally value AI support may not show disapproval (Meyers et al., 2026).

text.text: Our own exploratory data suggest that people who found AI empathy helpful expressed greater willingness to offload, while those who found friends or therapists more helpful showed greater indifference (see Table S5).

text.text: Younger people may also be more receptive to people seeking AI empathy.

Young people appear more open about discussing their mental health struggles and broadcasting how they seek support (Rüsch & Kösters, 2021), and they may also be less concerned (and judgmental) about empathic AI use.
text.formatted: Young people appear more open about discussing their mental health struggles and broadcasting how they seek support <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rüsch & Kösters, 2021)</ref>, and they may also be less concerned (and judgmental) about empathic AI use.

text.text: Who is seeking support also shapes how much empathy observers can give or offload to AI.

Someone may not be worried about their acquaintance going to AI for empathy if they are technologically competent, while the same behavior in someone who is seen as less tech-savvy may elicit stronger disapproval (Meyers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Someone may not be worried about their acquaintance going to AI for empathy if they are technologically competent, while the same behavior in someone who is seen as less tech-savvy may elicit stronger disapproval <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Meyers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The closeness of the relationship between empathy givers and seekers also likely plays a pivotal role.

Offloading empathy when a close friend is struggling may feel more like a betrayal of relational duty (Finkel et al., 2002) than the same behavior toward a casual acquaintance, where obligations to give empathy are weaker.
text.formatted: Offloading empathy when a close friend is struggling may feel more like a betrayal of relational duty <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Finkel et al., 2002)</ref> than the same behavior toward a casual acquaintance, where obligations to give empathy are weaker.

text.text: Additionally, people may choose to offload empathy (or communicate disapproval), depending on the reason why someone is seeking AI empathy.

People turn to AI for concerns ranging from everyday anxiety to serious mental health struggles and abusive situations (Huang et al., 2026), and empathy givers may be less likely to offload if someone really needs help, such as in a serious crisis.
text.formatted: People turn to AI for concerns ranging from everyday anxiety to serious mental health struggles and abusive situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Huang et al., 2026)</ref>, and empathy givers may be less likely to offload if someone really needs help, such as in a serious crisis.

text.text: But for less serious situations, like everyday stress or minor frustrations, people may be more willing to offload.
We recruited U.S. participants, but different cultural contexts likely shape differences in empathy offloading and social judgment behaviors.

Western countries tend to be more skeptical of AI while Eastern cultures tend to be more trusting and optimistic about AI (Gillespie et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), suggesting that perceived capacity for AI empathy-and consequently, empathy offloading-may be higher in Eastern cultures.

text.text: At the same time, people in more collectivist cultures display higher empathic concern and stronger felt obligations toward others (Chopik et al., 2017; Markus & Kitayama, 1991), which could prevent offloading even when AI is trusted.
text.formatted: At the same time, people in more collectivist cultures display higher empathic concern and stronger felt obligations toward others <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chopik et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Markus & Kitayama, 1991)</ref>, which could prevent offloading even when AI is trusted.

text.text: Whether greater trust in AI or stronger felt obligation to provide human empathy dominates-and whether norms around support amplify or decrease social judgment toward AI-seekers-remains an open question.
Future work should test empathy offloading effects beyond Western populations to understand when empathic AI leads to offloading behaviors.
Before deciding to offload emotional support to AI, someone must first become aware that someone they know has sought AI empathy.

While people often keep their empathy-seeking private (Gross & John, 2003; Vogel & Wade, 2009), some are publicly disclosing their use of empathic AI in online communities like Reddit (Huang et al., 2026), and perhaps they will soon disclose to friends and family.

text.text: Our two study designs capture two potential routes through which such awareness likely spreads: Study 2 tests how people learn about empathic AI from the media, and Study 3 tests observers learning about another's AIseeking in a personal context.
As AI emotional support becomes more visible and discussed, the situations we study here will only become more common, making the ethical questions they raise more urgent to explore.
AI is changing how we live with one another.
LLMs already draft our emails and edit our prose.
But, with the rise of empathic AI, machines replace not just human cognition, but human empathy.
For most of human history, providing emotional support was an ethical behavior that bound people together.
But now, we can offload this crucial interpersonal behavior to AI-and our data suggest that people are willing to let AI shoulder some of the burden of empathic support.
As empathic AI advances, the answer to the question "What do we owe each other?"
might be "less than before."
